events.title: Jomon pottery begins
events.description: Hunter-gatherers on the archipelago begin making cord-marked earthenware, among the oldest pottery found anywhere. The Jomon culture that takes its name from it lasts more than ten thousand years.

events.title: Sannai-Maruyama settled
events.description: A large permanent settlement in northern Honshu, with pit dwellings, storage pits and a chestnut grove under management. It undercuts the idea that farming is a precondition for settled life.

events.title: Wet rice cultivation arrives
events.description: Paddy rice, bronze and iron reach northern Kyushu from the Korean peninsula. The Yayoi culture that follows reorganises society around the harvest and the storehouse.

events.title: Yoshinogari grows into a moated town
events.description: A large Yayoi settlement ringed by ditches and watchtowers. Fortification on this scale implies organised violence and something worth defending.

events.title: Chinese court grants a gold seal
events.description: The Han emperor sends a gold seal to the ruler of Na, in northern Kyushu. It is the first firmly dated Chinese record of contact with the islands.

events.title: Queen Himiko sends envoys to Wei
events.description: Chinese chronicles describe Himiko, a shaman-queen of Yamatai who rules by ritual authority and whose location is still argued over. She is the first named individual in Japanese history.

events.title: Keyhole tombs spread
events.description: Enormous mounded tombs in a distinctive keyhole shape appear across the Kinai region and beyond. Their uniformity suggests a single elite culture asserting itself over rivals.

events.title: Campaigns on the Korean peninsula
events.description: The Gwanggaeto stele records Wa forces fighting in Korea. Whatever the truth of the claims, the peninsula is where Japan gets its writing, its metallurgy and eventually its religion.

events.title: Buddhism reaches the court
events.description: The king of Baekje sends an image of the Buddha and sutras to the Yamato court. The gift triggers a factional fight over whether the foreign god will offend the native ones.

events.title: The Soga defeat the Mononobe
events.description: A short, decisive clan war settles the Buddhism question by force. The pro-Buddhist Soga win, and the new religion becomes state business.

events.title: The Seventeen-Article Constitution
events.description: Attributed to Prince Shotoku, it is less a constitution than a moral charter for officials, drawing on Confucian hierarchy and Buddhist ethics. Harmony is placed first.

events.title: Envoys sent to Sui China
events.description: A mission carries a letter addressing the Sui emperor as one sovereign to another. The presumption reportedly annoys him; the embassies continue anyway.

events.title: The Taika Reform
events.description: A palace coup removes the Soga and launches a programme of Chinese-style centralisation: land nationalised in principle, provinces surveyed, taxes standardised.

events.title: Defeat at the Baekgang River
events.description: A fleet sent to prop up Baekje is destroyed by Tang and Silla forces. Japan withdraws from the peninsula and starts fortifying its own coast.

events.title: The Taiho Code
events.description: A full legal code on the Tang model gives the state a written constitution of ranks, ministries and penalties. The system it describes outlasts the reality it describes.

events.title: Capital moves to Nara
events.description: Heijo-kyo is laid out on a grid copied from Chang'an. A permanent capital replaces the practice of moving after each emperor's death.

events.title: The Kojiki compiled
events.description: Japan's oldest surviving book records the myths of the gods and the descent of the imperial line from the sun goddess. It is history written to justify a dynasty.

events.title: The Great Buddha of Todai-ji dedicated
events.description: A bronze colossus consecrated in a ceremony attended by envoys from across Asia. The project nearly exhausts the country's copper and its labour levies.

events.title: Capital moves to Heian-kyo
events.description: The court relocates to what becomes Kyoto, partly to escape the political weight of Nara's monasteries. It stays the imperial seat for over a thousand years.

events.title: Embassies to China halted
events.description: Sugawara no Michizane argues the Tang is collapsing and the voyages are not worth the risk. Cut off from the model, court culture turns inward and becomes distinctly Japanese.

events.title: The Fujiwara at their height
events.description: Fujiwara no Michinaga governs through marriage, supplying empresses to successive emperors and ruling as grandfather to the throne. Formal office matters less than family position.

events.title: The Tale of Genji written
events.description: Murasaki Shikibu's court novel dissects a world of aesthetic obsession and thwarted feeling. It is arguably the first psychological novel anywhere.

events.title: The age of mappo begins
events.description: By a widely accepted reckoning the Latter Day of the Law starts this year, an era in which salvation by one's own effort is impossible. Pure Land devotion spreads accordingly.

events.title: The Hogen Disturbance
events.description: A succession quarrel is settled by warriors brought into the capital to fight it. The court discovers it cannot send them home again.

events.title: The Genpei War begins
events.description: The Minamoto rise against the dominant Taira. Five years of fighting end the aristocracy's monopoly on power.

events.title: Taira destroyed at Dan-no-ura
events.description: A sea battle in the straits annihilates the Taira; the child emperor drowns with the sword of the regalia. The Minamoto are left without rivals.

events.title: Minamoto no Yoritomo becomes shogun
events.description: A military government is established at Kamakura, deliberately far from the court. Japan now has an emperor who reigns and a shogun who rules.

events.title: The Jokyu War
events.description: A retired emperor tries to overthrow the shogunate and loses badly. Kamakura exiles him and starts appointing its own men to watch the capital.

events.title: The Goseibai Shikimoku
events.description: A short, practical law code for warriors, written in plain language and based on precedent rather than Chinese theory. It governs samurai society for centuries.

events.title: Nichiren begins preaching
events.description: A fiercely polemical monk insists the Lotus Sutra alone can save the country and that rival schools are ruining it. He is exiled twice and nearly executed.

events.title: First Mongol invasion
events.description: A Yuan fleet lands at Hakata Bay, fights a hard day and withdraws to its ships, where a storm scatters it. Japanese tactics prove badly suited to massed infantry.

events.title: Second Mongol invasion repelled
events.description: A far larger force is held off by a stone wall along the bay and then wrecked by a typhoon. The kamikaze, or divine wind, enters the national story permanently.

events.title: The Kamakura shogunate falls
events.description: Emperor Go-Daigo's revolt succeeds when the general sent to crush him changes sides. The Hojo regents kill themselves in their burning city.

events.title: The Ashikaga take power
events.description: Ashikaga Takauji breaks with Go-Daigo and installs a rival emperor, beginning a shogunate based in Kyoto and a sixty-year split in the imperial line.

events.title: The Golden Pavilion built
events.description: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu builds Kinkaku-ji as a retirement villa. His court patronises the tea ceremony and Noh theatre and sets a template for elite taste.

events.title: Tally trade with Ming China
events.description: Yoshimitsu accepts the title King of Japan from the Ming to secure licensed trade. Later shoguns find the vassal wording humiliating and the profits persuasive.

events.title: The Onin War begins
events.description: A succession dispute among the Ashikaga turns Kyoto into a battlefield for a decade. Central authority does not recover; the provinces go their own way.

events.title: Ikko-ikki seize Kaga province
events.description: A league of Pure Land believers, farmers and low-ranking samurai expels the governor and runs the province itself for nearly a century.

events.title: Portuguese arrive with firearms
events.description: A Chinese ship carrying Portuguese traders is blown onto Tanegashima. Local smiths copy the arquebus within a year and the technology spreads fast.

events.title: Francis Xavier lands at Kagoshima
events.description: The Jesuit mission begins. Within fifty years there are said to be several hundred thousand Christians, concentrated in Kyushu.

events.title: Oda Nobunaga wins at Okehazama
events.description: A minor lord ambushes a far larger army in a rainstorm and kills its commander. Nobunaga's rise dates from this one afternoon.

events.title: Mount Hiei burned
events.description: Nobunaga destroys the great Tendai monastery and kills thousands, ending the political and military power of the warrior monks.

events.title: Volley fire at Nagashino
events.description: Massed arquebuses behind palisades break the Takeda cavalry. The battle is remembered as the moment gunpowder settles Japanese warfare.

events.title: Nobunaga killed at Honno-ji
events.description: Betrayed by his own general Akechi Mitsuhide, Nobunaga dies in a burning temple with unification unfinished. Hideyoshi avenges him within a fortnight and inherits the project.

events.title: The sword hunt
events.description: Hideyoshi disarms the peasantry, ostensibly to melt the weapons into a Buddha image. The line between farmer and warrior becomes hereditary and legal.

events.title: Invasion of Korea
events.description: Hideyoshi launches an enormous army at Korea intending to go on to China. Two campaigns end in withdrawal, ruin for Korea and lasting resentment.

events.title: The twenty-six martyrs of Nagasaki
events.description: Hideyoshi has Christians crucified at Nagasaki as suspicion of foreign loyalty grows. Persecution becomes intermittent policy, then permanent.

events.title: Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara
events.description: A single day's fighting, decided by defections, leaves Ieyasu master of Japan. The losers' domains are broken up or moved to the margins.

events.title: The Tokugawa shogunate founded
events.description: Ieyasu takes the title of shogun and builds his capital at Edo. The settlement he imposes holds for two and a half centuries.

events.title: Osaka Castle falls
events.description: The last Toyotomi stronghold is taken and Hideyoshi's line extinguished. Laws issued the same year fix the duties of the court and the daimyo.

events.title: Alternate attendance made compulsory
events.description: Daimyo must spend alternate years in Edo and leave their families there permanently. The cost and the hostages make rebellion impractical.

events.title: The Shimabara Rebellion
events.description: Overtaxed peasants, many of them Christian, hold out in a ruined castle before being annihilated. Christianity is driven underground for two hundred years.

events.title: Sakoku: the country closed
events.description: Portuguese ships are banned and foreign contact is reduced to a Dutch and Chinese trading post at Nagasaki. Leaving the country becomes a capital offence.

events.title: The Great Fire of Meireki
events.description: Fire destroys most of Edo and kills perhaps a hundred thousand people. The rebuilt city is planned with firebreaks and becomes one of the largest in the world.

events.title: Genroku culture flourishes
events.description: Merchant wealth funds kabuki, woodblock prints and the novels of Ihara Saikaku. The floating world is a townsman's culture in a warrior's state.

events.title: The forty-seven ronin
events.description: Masterless samurai avenge their lord and are ordered to kill themselves. The episode becomes the defining story of loyalty against law.

events.title: The ban on Western books relaxed
events.description: Shogun Yoshimune permits imported works other than Christian ones. Rangaku, Dutch learning, gives a small class of scholars a window on European medicine and astronomy.

events.title: A Dutch anatomy text translated
events.description: Sugita Genpaku and colleagues translate a European anatomical atlas after checking it against a dissection. The accuracy of the drawings shocks them into rethinking Chinese medicine.

events.title: The Tenmei famine
events.description: Volcanic cold and crop failure kill hundreds of thousands over several years. Riots in the cities expose how thin the shogunate's competence has worn.

events.title: Order to drive off foreign ships
events.description: Foreign vessels approaching the coast are to be fired on without negotiation. The policy survives until it becomes obvious it cannot be enforced.

events.title: Perry's black ships arrive
events.description: An American squadron anchors in Edo Bay and demands the country open. The shogunate, unable to fight and unwilling to agree, asks the daimyo for advice and reveals its weakness.

events.title: The Convention of Kanagawa
events.description: Two ports are opened and an American consul admitted. Further treaties follow with tariffs Japan cannot set and courts it cannot control.

events.title: Ii Naosuke assassinated
events.description: The chief minister who signed the treaties and purged his critics is cut down outside Edo Castle. Political murder becomes a normal instrument.

events.title: Bombardment of Kagoshima
events.description: British warships shell Satsuma over the killing of a British merchant. Satsuma concludes that expelling the barbarians requires first becoming like them.

events.title: The Satsuma-Choshu alliance
events.description: Two domains that loathe each other are brokered into an alliance against the shogunate. Together they have the men, the money and the modern weapons.

events.title: The shogun resigns
events.description: Tokugawa Yoshinobu returns his authority to the emperor, hoping to keep a leading role in whatever comes next. His opponents make sure he does not.

events.title: The Meiji Restoration
events.description: The emperor is declared restored to direct rule and the capital moves to Tokyo. A small group of young samurai from the western domains now runs the country.

events.title: The Boshin War ends at Hakodate
events.description: The last Tokugawa loyalists surrender in Hokkaido after declaring a short-lived republic. Resistance to the new government is over.

events.title: The domains abolished
events.description: Two hundred and sixty domains become prefectures with governors appointed from Tokyo. The daimyo are pensioned off with startlingly little resistance.

events.title: Compulsory education proclaimed
events.description: Universal primary schooling is decreed, along with the first railway and a Western calendar. Literacy rates rise fast from an already high base.

events.title: Conscription and the land tax
events.description: Military service is extended to commoners and the land tax is fixed in cash rather than rice. Both reforms provoke riots and both hold.

events.title: The Satsuma Rebellion
events.description: Saigo Takamori leads disaffected samurai against the government he helped create. A conscript army beats them, settling the question of who fights for Japan.

events.title: The Ryukyu Kingdom annexed
events.description: Okinawa becomes a prefecture and its king is removed to Tokyo. The islands are governed as a periphery and their language suppressed in schools.

events.title: The Meiji Constitution
events.description: A constitution modelled on Prussia's grants an elected lower house while reserving sovereignty to the emperor. The army reports to him, not to the cabinet.

events.title: War with Qing China
events.description: A quarrel over Korea becomes a war Japan wins decisively at sea and on land. Taiwan is ceded and Japan acquires its first colony.

events.title: The Triple Intervention
events.description: Russia, France and Germany force Japan to hand back the Liaodong peninsula. The humiliation is used to justify a decade of military spending.

events.title: The Ainu protection act
events.description: Legislation reclassifies Ainu land, pushes farming on hunting communities and bans their language in schools. It is repealed only in 1997.

events.title: The Anglo-Japanese Alliance
events.description: Britain allies with a non-European power on equal terms for the first time. It ends Japan's diplomatic isolation and frees its hand against Russia.

events.title: War with Russia
events.description: Japan attacks Port Arthur and grinds through a year of siege and mass casualties on land.

events.title: Victory at Tsushima
events.description: Togo's fleet destroys the Russian Baltic squadron in the straits. An Asian power has beaten a European empire, and the news travels across the colonised world.

events.title: Korea annexed
events.description: Korea is absorbed outright after five years as a protectorate. Thirty-five years of colonial rule follow.

events.title: Tariff autonomy regained
events.description: The last of the unequal treaty provisions is renegotiated away. The central foreign-policy goal of the Meiji period is complete.

events.title: The Taisho era begins
events.description: The Meiji emperor dies and his frail son succeeds. Real power drifts from the ageing oligarchs towards parties, bureaucrats and the press.

events.title: Japan enters the First World War
events.description: Japan takes German possessions in China and the Pacific at small cost and sells to the Allies at great profit. The economy booms.

events.title: The rice riots
events.description: Price rises set off nationwide unrest that brings down the cabinet. The first commoner prime minister takes office in its aftermath.

events.title: The racial equality proposal rejected
events.description: Japan's clause on racial equality at Versailles wins a majority and is vetoed by the chair. The snub is remembered bitterly for decades.

events.title: The Great Kanto Earthquake
events.description: Tokyo and Yokohama burn and over a hundred thousand people die. In the chaos, thousands of Koreans are murdered by vigilantes acting on rumour.

events.title: Universal male suffrage and the Peace Preservation Law
events.description: The vote is extended to all adult men and, in the same session, a law is passed to crush political dissent. Democratisation and repression arrive together.

events.title: The Showa financial crisis
events.description: Bank runs and failures follow years of unresolved bad debt from the wartime boom. Rural distress deepens and the parties get the blame.

events.title: The Manchurian Incident
events.description: Officers of the Kwantung Army stage an explosion on a railway and seize Manchuria without orders from Tokyo. The government follows rather than disciplines them.

events.title: Prime Minister Inukai assassinated
events.description: Young naval officers murder the prime minister in his residence. Party cabinets effectively end; the killers receive light sentences after a public sympathy campaign.

events.title: Japan leaves the League of Nations
events.description: Rather than accept the League's finding on Manchuria, the delegation walks out. Diplomatic isolation is chosen deliberately.

events.title: The February 26 Incident
events.description: A mutiny by army officers seizes central Tokyo and kills several ministers before the emperor demands its suppression. The army emerges stronger from having crushed it.

events.title: Full-scale war with China
events.description: A clash at the Marco Polo Bridge escalates into an undeclared war that never ends until 1945. Japan takes the cities and cannot hold the country.

events.title: The Nanjing Massacre
events.description: Japanese forces take the Chinese capital and commit mass killing and rape over several weeks. It remains the sharpest wound in the relationship.

events.title: The Tripartite Pact
events.description: Japan aligns formally with Germany and Italy and moves into northern Indochina. American oil and scrap exports are progressively cut off in response.

events.title: Pearl Harbor
events.description: Carrier aircraft strike the US Pacific Fleet while Japan sweeps through Southeast Asia. The war becomes global and, in the long run, unwinnable.

events.title: Defeat at Midway
events.description: Four carriers are lost in a day. The initiative passes to the United States barely six months after Pearl Harbor.

events.title: The fall of Saipan
events.description: The loss of the Marianas puts the home islands within bomber range and brings down the Tojo cabinet.

events.title: The firebombing of Tokyo
events.description: A single night's incendiary raid kills around a hundred thousand people and burns out much of the city. Sixty other cities follow.

events.title: The Battle of Okinawa ends
events.description: Nearly three months of fighting kill perhaps a quarter of the island's civilians, many in mass suicides urged on them by Japanese troops.

events.title: Hiroshima
events.description: An atomic bomb destroys the city and kills tens of thousands instantly, with many more dying later of burns and radiation.

events.title: Nagasaki
events.description: A second bomb falls as the Soviet Union declares war and invades Manchuria. The two shocks arrive within days of each other.

events.title: The emperor broadcasts surrender
events.description: Hirohito's voice is heard by his subjects for the first time, telling them to endure the unendurable. Japan has lost around three million dead.

events.title: The new constitution
events.description: Drafted largely by the occupation, it makes the emperor a symbol, guarantees civil rights and renounces war in Article 9. It has never been amended.

events.title: Land reform and the zaibatsu broken up
events.description: Tenant farmers are turned into owners and the great industrial combines are formally dissolved. Rural politics is transformed; the combines quietly reassemble.

events.title: The San Francisco Peace Treaty
events.description: Japan regains sovereignty and simultaneously signs a security treaty keeping American bases. The two documents define the postwar settlement.

events.title: The Liberal Democratic Party formed
events.description: Conservative parties merge and proceed to govern almost without interruption. Politics becomes competition between factions inside one party.

events.title: Protests against the security treaty
events.description: Enormous demonstrations against the revised US treaty force the prime minister out, though the treaty passes. The government pivots to promising income growth instead.

events.title: The Tokyo Olympics
events.description: The Games and the new bullet train announce recovery to the world. Growth runs near ten per cent a year through the decade.

events.title: Second-largest economy in the world
events.description: Japan passes West Germany in output. Pollution scandals such as Minamata disease show what the growth has cost.

events.title: Okinawa returned
events.description: Administration reverts to Japan after twenty-seven years of American rule, though the bases stay. Relations with China are normalised the same year.

events.title: The oil shock
events.description: Quadrupled crude prices end the era of double-digit growth and force a shift to energy efficiency and higher-value exports.

events.title: The Plaza Accord
events.description: Coordinated intervention drives the yen sharply higher. Easy money to cushion exporters inflates land and share prices instead.

events.title: The Showa era ends at the market peak
events.description: Hirohito dies in January and the Nikkei tops out in December at almost 39,000. Neither the reign nor the boom is repeated.

events.title: The bubble bursts
events.description: Land and equity prices collapse, leaving banks with bad loans they will not write off. What follows is called the lost decade and then extended.

events.title: The Kobe earthquake and the sarin attack
events.description: Six thousand die in the January quake; in March the Aum Shinrikyo cult releases nerve gas on the Tokyo subway. Confidence in official competence takes a lasting hit.

events.title: The LDP loses power
events.description: The Democratic Party wins a landslide after half a century of near-continuous conservative rule. It governs for three difficult years.

events.title: Tohoku earthquake and Fukushima
events.description: A magnitude nine quake and tsunami kill nearly twenty thousand people and cause meltdowns at the Fukushima Daiichi plant. Every reactor in the country is shut down.

events.title: Abenomics begins
events.description: Shinzo Abe returns to office promising monetary easing, fiscal spending and structural reform. Deflation eases; the debt and the demographics do not.

events.title: The Reiwa era begins
events.description: Akihito abdicates, the first emperor to do so in two centuries, and Naruhito succeeds him.

events.title: Shinzo Abe assassinated
events.description: Japan's longest-serving prime minister is shot at a campaign stop in Nara. The investigation exposes the Unification Church's reach into the governing party.

events.title: The Nikkei finally passes its 1989 peak
events.description: Thirty-four years after the bubble burst, the index sets a new record. In the same period the population has begun falling in earnest.
